body: The horses get fed before anything else happens and they do not care what day it is, which is why a woman is standing in a yard at ten to five with a coat over her pyjamas, waiting for a kettle in the tack room. There is no light to speak of, only a grey strip over the hedge that could be weather. One of the two is banging the door with a hoof, which he does every morning and has never once been rewarded for. She is thinking about a shoe, and whether the farrier said Thursday or Friday, and that the yard tap will freeze again if this goes on.
None of that is the start of a day. It is a joining-in. Whatever the day is, it was running when she came out, it was running while she was asleep, and the horse had been awake in it for some time.

Genesis reports each day in an order most readers slide straight past. Evening first. Then morning. Then the day is counted and closed. On that reckoning a day does not begin when you wake up and get to work on it.

It is worth taking the sentence at its word, because a great deal follows. If the day turns at dusk, the first thing that happens in any day is that the light goes and people stop working. The second is that they sleep. The opening act of a day, structurally, is unconsciousness — several hours in which you contribute nothing and it proceeds without you. By the time you are upright it is well advanced. This is why the feasts begin in the evening, and why Shabbat starts on a Friday at dusk rather than a Saturday at breakfast: the rest comes at the front.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today. HM 380.80 is Heaven’s Dawn, assigned and in build and not yet on air, an early-morning devotional station with First Light at five and Daily Bread at half past six in its published schedule. Its three towers are Boston, Kansas City and Seattle, chosen in that order so that first light rolls west across them.

Two things about that schedule should be said exactly, because it would be easy to claim more than is true. The times are clock times at each of its bases; nothing is computed against the horizon outside your window. And First Light is at five, which most of the year is well before there is any light. That is the deliberate part, and it costs something: a station wanting an audience would put its best hour at eight. And there was evening, and there was morning — the first day. The order in that sentence is not decorative, and a schedule that believed it would look like this one.

The alternative reckoning is so ordinary now that it is invisible. The day begins when the alarm goes and you pick up the phone; it is a container handed to you empty, and its quality is a verdict on how well you filled it. Nothing about that is wicked, and it gets a great deal done. But it puts the whole weight of the day on the person who wakes up into it, and it quietly makes sleep into the thing that comes afterwards, on account of what you spent. Rest as wages. You have to earn the right to stop.

The band is arranged so that hours are real rather than decorative. Stations carry blocks at their own local clock — a morning block, an evening block — and both are published before they air, so the day file exists in advance and is the same for everybody tuned there. Two people on the same number at the same second are in the same hour of the same day. That is what makes a schedule a schedule rather than a queue, and it is why a station can put something before dawn on purpose and have it mean something.
There is a version of the early morning that is currently very popular, and it is not the same thing at all.

The productivity morning deserves more credit than people like me usually give it. Getting up at five and doing the hard thing first genuinely works, the discipline is real, and the church has often been slack about ordinary diligence while eloquent about rest. Plenty of people have got their lives back that way. But look where it puts the weight. The early rise is an act of will, performed by you, to seize a day that would otherwise have got away — so a morning you fail to seize is a morning lost, the failure is yours, and it accumulates. It is the same container, filled more efficiently. Genesis is not asking you to seize anything. It is telling you the day started without you.
A day you did not start is a day you cannot fail to start.

A woman of sixty-eight lies awake and listens to her husband go downstairs at ten past four, which he has done nearly every morning since the spring. He does not sleep past four now and will not lie there wanting to. She hears the third stair, the kitchen door, and then, after a few minutes, something quiet through the floor from the front room — not the words, only the shape of it. She does not go down. Twice she has, and it was wrong; he needs the hour on his own. At about half five he comes back up with two mugs of tea and gets in beside her, and they drink them, and the window turns from black to grey to a colour.
Nobody in that house started a day. Something was already going when he came down, and had been going while they slept. His part was to sit down inside it.

The honest cost of keeping the older reckoning is that nothing around you keeps it. Your employer does not. The school does not. Your calendar turns over at midnight in the middle of your night, so you are permanently half a day out of step with the people you live among. And the station this article is named for is not on air yet: HM 380.80 is assigned and in build, so this is an argument about how a day file will be built, not something you can put on tonight.

But being out of step is the content, not the inconvenience. A reckoning that agreed with the calendar on your phone would correct nothing, because it is that calendar teaching you the day is yours to launch and yours to have wasted. The disagreement is where the disposition lives. Rest at the front of a day rather than the end of it is not a scheduling preference; it is the difference between sleeping because you have finished and sleeping because it is the first thing you were given to do.

So a station that airs before sunrise is not making an atmospheric choice about gentle music in the half dark. It is keeping time by a different clock, and saying so in the only way a broadcast can say anything, which is by what it puts on and when. The turn happens in the dark. What plays before first light is the beginning of a day rather than the tail of the last one, and anyone awake at that hour is joining something that started without them.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing.

Four kinds of programming run on this dial and it is worth knowing they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. A good many carry a morning block and an evening block, which is the sentence from Genesis printed across most of the dial.

So while the dawn station is being built, start at HM 329.00 — Israel Inspire. It is Hebrew-language worship, sung in the names the Scriptures use, and it is a small station still filling out. It earns the recommendation here because its day is the argument. Its morning block is shir shel shachar, a song of dawn; its evening block, at eight at night, is tehilat erev, the praise of evening. Those are the two ends of the sentence this article has been about, in the language the sentence was written in, on a frequency where they are ordinary scheduling rather than a point being made. You will not follow the words. You are not required to.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

Take that as an invitation rather than an instruction. Do not set an alarm for it and do not make a discipline of it. But the next time you are up before the light — and everybody is, sooner or later, for one reason or another — put HM 329.00 on quietly before you do anything else, and notice that it was playing before you got there. That is the whole of the argument, and it takes about a minute to check.
